Chapter 4: How Society Shapes Gender From the Start.
Picture this: in a hospital nursery, newborns are lined up side by side, wrapped in identical blankets. If you were to look in, you’d probably see just tiny, fragile babies—full of possibility and not much else to tell them apart. But here’s the thing—right from the very first moments, the world starts treating them differently. Visitors might fawn over the “strong little man” or the “sweet little girl,” already projecting hopes, dreams, and expectations on these brand-new humans. It’s so automatic, most of us don’t even notice it’s happening.
And as those days turn into months, those small differences start to add up. Parents—often without even realizing it—might push their sons to be more adventurous, to take risks, to get a little dirty. Daughters, on the other hand, might hear more reminders to be careful, to be gentle. When it’s time to pick out toys? Trucks and building blocks almost always go to the boys, while dolls and kitchen sets end up in the girls’ baskets. Even the way grown-ups talk to kids can shift—boys get praised for being tough, girls for being pretty or polite.
All these early experiences? They have a real impact. Kids are like little sponges—they soak up every cue, every comment, learning what’s expected of them and what’s truly valued. Think about it: a little girl who’s told she’s “not a math person” might just stop trying, even if she actually loves solving puzzles. A boy who’s discouraged from showing emotion might learn to keep everything inside—maybe even believing that being vulnerable makes him weak.
And it’s not just happening at home. Schools play a big role, too. Teachers, without meaning to, might call on boys more in science class, or assume girls are naturals at reading. The textbooks and classroom stories? They can reinforce old stereotypes, showing men as leaders and women as helpers. Even on the playground, games often split by gender—boys get pushed to compete, while girls are nudged to cooperate.
These patterns are so deeply woven into our lives that they can feel completely natural—almost like they’re just the way things are. But when researchers actually dig into the data, they find something surprising: the differences between boys and girls are much smaller than most of us think. In fact, there’s often more variation within each group than there is between them. That whole idea that boys are born better at math, or girls are naturally more empathetic? It doesn’t really hold up.
What usually gets missed is just how much opportunity and encouragement matter. When kids get the chance to try new things—without anyone telling them what’s “for boys” or “for girls”—they can surprise everyone. A girl who’s handed a set of blocks might develop some seriously strong spatial skills. A boy who’s free to talk about his feelings? He might grow up to be more empathetic and caring.
Socialization is subtle, but it’s powerful. It shapes not just what kids do, but how they see themselves—and what they believe is possible for their future. Over time, those beliefs can become self-fulfilling prophecies, steering choices and shaping lives.
But here’s the good news: change is absolutely possible. When parents, teachers, and even whole communities start to notice these patterns, they can challenge them. By creating spaces where diversity is valued and exploration is encouraged, we can start to break down the walls that box kids in. It’s not always easy, but the payoff is huge—a world where everyone, no matter their gender, gets to discover who they really are.
